we-the-people-1787-1791.works: The pop-up sets out the three-fifths clause plainly and without commentary: people counted under the clause, seats in 1793, and seats if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all, with National Archives and Census Bureau credits. That is a factual, sourced treatment I can defend. The pies make the free/enslaved split visible at a glance, and the North Carolina pop-up answers 'why two pies' directly.

findings.where: Population in 1790 pop-up, Virginia (q1-virginia); Q1 step 3 (percentage enslaved), also read in Q3
findings.what: The first line reads '292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%)'. My students will copy that number down, and it looks like a glitch on the very figure I most need to look careful.
findings.why: Q1 asks students to compare this percentage with a quarter. On the slavery figures above all, a parent or district reviewer who sees a broken number will start questioning the rest of the data.
findings.suggestion: Format the percentage field to one decimal place (39.1%) in the pop-up for every state.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png; pop-up text '292,627 of them enslaved (39.099998474121094%)'

findings.where: Attribution line at the bottom of every view (open, q1-virginia, q2-seats); Population in 1790 layer; Q1 and Q3
findings.what: The credits at the bottom say '1790 census figures: Wikipedia (from Census Bureau volumes)'. The pop-up credits the National Archives for seats and the Census Bureau for the ratio, but the census counts themselves come from Wikipedia.
findings.why: The enslaved counts and the three-fifths numbers are exactly what a parent complaint would challenge. I can defend 'U.S. Census Bureau, 1790 census'. I cannot defend Wikipedia in a district review.
findings.suggestion: Check the 1790 figures against the Census Bureau's own 1790 census publication, cite that in the attribution instead of Wikipedia, and add 'Census: U.S. Census Bureau, 1790' to the pop-up's source line.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--open.png and --q1-virginia.png attribution bar; pop-up source line 'Seats: National Archives · Ratio: U.S. Census Bureau'

findings.where: House seats in 1793 view (q2-seats); Q2 steps 2-3 (read the labels: most and fewest seats), Q3
findings.what: With House seats on, I see seat labels like 'VA: 19', 'PA: 13', 'NY: 10', 'KY: 2', 'GA: 2'. But I also see dark blue and orange pies labelled 'VA 10', 'NC 12', 'NC (1788)', 'SC 8', 'NH 9', 'RI 13'. Those are the order of ratification, not seats. I can't find a seat label for Delaware, Rhode Island, New Jersey, Maryland, South Carolina or Massachusetts, so 'DE: 1', the fewest, isn't on screen. The population pies are faint under the blue shading.
findings.why: Students will read 'VA 10' or 'RI 13' as seat counts and get Q2 wrong. The fewest-seats answer depends on a label that isn't showing, and the palest shading (1 to 2 seats) can't tell Delaware's 1 from the states with 2.
findings.suggestion: Check whether Ratifying the Constitution really draws when only House seats in 1793 is turned on (the legend for this view doesn't list it), and fix that if so. Let the small states' seat labels show (allow overlap or use leader lines), or make 1 seat its own legend class. Add to Q2 step 2: 'If you can't see a state's label, click the state.'
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q2-seats.png; legend text lists only House seats in 1793 and Population in 1790

findings.where: Ratifying the Constitution layer (q4-ratify); Q4 steps 3-4 (which three votes were closest)
findings.what: In New England the pies pile on top of each other. The 'RI 13' label sits on the big Massachusetts pie, 'VT 14' sits beside a different pie, and there are no labels at all for MA 6, CT 5, NJ 3 or DE 1. Two of the three closest votes, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, are in that pile. The state outlines disappear when Population in 1790 is turned off, and there are no place names.
findings.why: Students will click the wrong pie or miss Massachusetts altogether. With no outlines or names, the only way to tell the pies apart is to click every one.
findings.suggestion: Add 'Open the New England and New York bookmark' to Q4 between steps 2 and 3, and check that every label shows at that bookmark. Keep the state outlines on as a separate outline-only layer when Population in 1790 is turned off.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-ratify.png

findings.where: Ratifying the Constitution, NC 12 pop-up (q4-nc); Q4 step 4 (why North Carolina has two pies)
findings.what: The pop-up says the Hillsborough convention 'voted 184 to 83 against ratifying', and the date reads '11/21/1789, 12:00 AM'.
findings.why: My understanding is that Hillsborough voted to neither ratify nor reject until amendments were proposed, and I have seen the vote given as 184 to 84. If a student or parent looks it up, 'against ratifying' is a simplification I'd have to explain. The '12:00 AM' looks like a computer error.
findings.suggestion: Check the Hillsborough vote and its wording against the Center for the Study of the American Constitution source the pop-up already cites. If confirmed, reword it to say the convention voted to neither ratify nor reject until amendments were proposed. Show all ratification dates as 'November 21, 1789', with no time.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q4-nc.png; pop-up text 'Ratified on 11/21/1789, 12:00 AM' and 'voted 184 to 83 against ratifying'

findings.where: Population in 1790 pop-up first line (q1-virginia, q2-seats) and the sheet's Reading the map ('Pies on the states show the people in 1790'); Q1, Q3
findings.what: The pop-up says '1790 census: 747,610 people', and the sheet calls this 'the people in 1790'. Nothing says that the census left out Native people living in their own nations, even though Cherokee and Creek lands lie inside today's outlines of Georgia, the Carolinas and Kentucky on this map.
findings.why: I need Native nations treated factually. Calling the census totals 'the people' erases them. The Constitution's own apportionment clause, which excluded 'Indians not taxed', is right on topic for Q3.
findings.suggestion: Add one sentence to the pop-up's note: 'The census did not count Native people living in their own nations (the Constitution's Indians not taxed).' Change the sheet to 'the people the census counted in 1790'.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--q1-virginia.png; pop-up text '1790 census: 747,610 people'

findings.where: Legend for Population in 1790 (open) and Ratifying the Constitution (q4-ratify); Q1, Q4
findings.what: The population size key is headed 'Total1790' and the ratification one just 'Total'. Both pie legends list a gray 'Other' that never appears in any pie.
findings.why: Students will ask what 'Other' means on a free/enslaved pie, and I don't want to answer that by guessing. 'Total' doesn't say that it means people in one layer and convention delegates in the other.
findings.suggestion: Rename the size keys 'People in 1790' and 'Delegates voting', and remove the 'Other' entry from both pie legends.
findings.evidence: we-the-people-1787-1791--open.png and --q4-ratify.png; legend text 'Total1790', 'Total', 'Other'

rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-liv.works: The district pop-up gives the representative, party and district number in one plain, neutral sentence, and the blue outlines show district edges clearly once you zoom in on a town. The National Register pop-up gives the place's name, address and type, with a National Archives link, a source I can point parents to.

findings.where: Congressional districts (119th Congress) pop-up (q1-district); Q1 step 3 (who represents your district, party, district number)
findings.what: The pop-up reads 'Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15', with no date. In Texas, the district lines on the November 2026 ballot are not the ones on this map. Only the teacher notes say so, not the pop-up or the sheet.
findings.why: We'll be doing this lesson right around the election. If a student tells their family 'we're in District X' from this map and the ballot says otherwise, I'll get a parent call. Names and parties are politically sensitive, so they need a date.
findings.suggestion: Add a line to the pop-up: '119th Congress (2025–2027), as of [layer update date]. In Texas and some other states, the districts for the November 2026 election are different.' Add the same caution to the sheet's Reading the map.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q1-district.png; pop-up text 'Mike Carey (Republican) represents Ohio Congressional District 15'

findings.where: Map zoomed out to the whole country or state (open); Q1 step 4 (how many districts does your state have)
findings.what: Zoomed out, the blue outlines around Houston and Dallas–Fort Worth run together into solid blue. Counting 38 Texas districts from that view isn't realistic.
findings.why: Students will guess or give up, and the count is part of the written answer.
findings.suggestion: Put the state's total in the pop-up ('one of Texas's 38 districts'), or change the sheet to 'Click a district and read how many districts your state has in the pop-up.'
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--open.png

findings.where: National Register of Historic Places pop-up (q4-nrhp-click); sheet Reading the map and Q4 step 3
findings.what: The sheet says these pop-ups 'give an address but not a name' and sends students to the basemap label or the National Archives link. The pop-up I got has the title 'Ohio Statehouse'.
findings.why: That's good news for students. But when the sheet contradicts the screen, students stop trusting the instructions, and the extra step wastes time.
findings.suggestion: Change the sheet (and About this map) to 'The pop-up title gives the place's name; below it are the address and type.' Keep the basemap label and the National Archives link only as a fallback.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png; pop-up text 'Ohio Statehouse / Property ID: 72001011'

findings.where: National Register of Historic Places layer (q4-nrhp-click); Q4 steps 2-3 (two diamonds nearest the school; read the name under the diamond)
findings.what: The diamond that opened 'Ohio Statehouse, SE corner of High and Broad Sts.' sits on High Street south of the I-70/I-71 interchange, near the Brewery District, well south of Broad Street. The pop-up also says 1 of 2.
findings.why: If the diamonds sit away from the real buildings, 'read the basemap label under the diamond' gives students the wrong name, and 'the two nearest your school' may not be.
findings.suggestion: I'd check the Statehouse point against its address. If the National Register points are only approximate, say so on the sheet: 'Diamonds can be a few blocks off: trust the name and address in the pop-up.'
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp-click.png

findings.where: National Register of Historic Places legend (q4-nrhp); Q4 step 4 (use the legend to tell a building from a district or a site)
findings.what: In the legend, 'district' is a brownish red and 'site' a dark red, while 'structure' and 'object' are a pale yellow-green and a gray that would disappear on this light basemap. Every diamond I can see downtown is the same dark teal, so I couldn't check how the others look on the map.
findings.why: Step 4 asks students to sort places by color. Two near-identical reds and two pale colors make that unreliable, and color alone fails any color-blind student.
findings.suggestion: Give the five types clearly different colors and shapes. Since the pop-up already says 'Resource Type: building', add to step 4: 'or read Resource Type in the pop-up'.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png; legend text 'building, structure, district, site, object'; pop-up 'Resource Type: building'

findings.where: Topographic basemap at close zoom; Q2 steps 1-2 and Q3 (find a courthouse, city hall, library and so on from basemap names)
findings.what: Even at the street-level view of downtown Columbus (q4-nrhp), the basemap names parks and neighborhoods but not the Statehouse, a courthouse or a library. I haven't seen a closer zoom, and I don't know whether small Texas towns get building labels at all.
findings.why: Q2 and Q3 depend entirely on students finding public buildings on the basemap. If my town's courthouse isn't labelled, those questions stall.
findings.suggestion: I'd zoom to our own town before teaching to check. Consider adding a points layer of courthouses, city halls, post offices and libraries, or let the sheet say students may pin a public place they know even if the basemap doesn't name it.
findings.evidence: rights-and-responsibilities-where-we-live--q4-nrhp.png (no building names at that zoom); closer zoom not pictured

presidential-elections-1796-1800.works: The 1796 pies, the legend and the pop-up title ('Pennsylvania: 15 electors') make a Federalist North and a Democratic-Republican South easy to see, and the pop-up explains the two-votes rule. The McCulloch pop-up (Question, Ruling, Why it matters, Why here, Source) is clear, neutral and sourced, just what I want.

findings.where: Landmark Supreme Court cases layer, Marbury v. Madison square, zoomed in on Washington and Baltimore (q4-marbury); Q4 steps 1-2 (read the Why here part)
findings.what: I clicked the Marbury v. Madison square and nothing opened. The McCulloch v. Maryland square does open its pop-up.
findings.why: Half of Q4 ('What happened in each place to bring the case to the Court?') can't be answered from the map, and my step 2 at the front of the class fails with everyone watching.
findings.suggestion: Check that the Marbury feature has its pop-up turned on and that the feature sits exactly under the square (its label and Maryland's pie are right beside it). Test the click at the zoomed-in view and at the opening view.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q4-marbury.png; '(no pop-up opened)'

findings.where: Election of 1796 layer at the opening view / The sixteen states bookmark (open, q1-pie); Q1 step 3 (click each two-color pie)
findings.what: Maryland's pie, the only split state Adams won, sits under the two pink court squares and the 'Marbury v. Madison (1803)' label, and the Delaware and New Jersey pies overlap it. At this scale the McCulloch label doesn't show at all.
findings.why: Students who click Maryland will get a court case or nothing, and some will leave Maryland off their list of split states, which is a key answer.
findings.suggestion: Have the Supreme Court cases layer off when the map opens and tell students to turn it on in Q4. Or add to Q1: 'Zoom in on Maryland to click its pie.'
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png and --q1-pie.png

findings.where: Election of 1796 pies for Virginia and Pennsylvania (open); Q1 answer (which states split their votes)
findings.what: Virginia's single Adams vote is a hairline orange sliver on a big blue pie, and Pennsylvania's is barely wider.
findings.why: Students hunting for 'two-color pies' will probably miss Virginia, which the answer notes count as one of the four split states.
findings.suggestion: Add to Q1 step 3: 'Some pies have only a thin orange slice. Look closely at Virginia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina.' Or label split states with their votes (e.g. 'VA 20–1').
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--open.png

findings.where: Switching Election of 1796 off and Election of 1800 on (q2-1800); Q2 step 1 and Q3 step 1
findings.what: After I switched layers, the Pennsylvania pop-up I had open still said 'Electors' votes in 1796: … Thomas Jefferson 14', with the 1800 pies behind it. The picture also caught the pies partway through changing, so I couldn't check the 1800 two-color pies themselves.
findings.why: Students will copy the 1796 numbers into their 1800 answers, especially for Pennsylvania, which goes from 14–1 to 8–7.
findings.suggestion: Add 'Close any open pop-up first' to step 1 of Q2 and Q3.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q2-1800.png; pop-up text 'Electors' votes in 1796' shown with the Election of 1800 legend

findings.where: Sheet Q1 answer ('Which part of the country mostly voted for Adams') compared with the pop-up's 'Electors' votes in 1796' (q1-pie)
findings.what: The map shows electors' votes, but the question asks which part of the country 'voted for' Adams.
findings.why: In 1796 many state legislatures, not voters, chose the electors. A student or parent could come away thinking the public voted this way. I'd check how many states chose electors by popular vote that year.
findings.suggestion: Reword it as 'In which part of the country did electors mostly vote for Adams, and in which for Jefferson?'
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-pie.png; pop-up text 'Electors' votes in 1796'

findings.where: Election of 1796 pop-up (q1-pie) and Supreme Court legend entry (open)
findings.what: The pop-up says 'John Adams (Federalist), 1 votes'. The Supreme Court legend shows a pink square with no words beside it.
findings.why: These are small, but careless wording is the first thing a reviewer notices.
findings.suggestion: Write '1 vote' when the count is 1, and label the legend square 'Supreme Court case'.
findings.evidence: presidential-elections-1796-1800--q1-pie.png ('1 votes'); --open.png legend

louisiana-purchase-1803-1806.works: The yellow purchase beside the land of 1783 shows the country roughly doubling at a glance. At the Across the Rockies bookmark it's clear where the trail leaves the yellow and that the Pacific Northwest is unshaded. The sheet's Before you start and Looking back deal honestly with Native nations, which helps me defend the lesson.

findings.where: Biomes layer at the Up the Missouri bookmark (q3-biomes) compared with the zoomed-out view (q3-biome-click); Q3 steps 3-4 (click the shading along the route)
findings.what: At the Up the Missouri bookmark with Biomes on, I see no biome colors, only the yellow purchase, the Texas and Mexican Cession colors, brown watershed lines and a watershed pop-up ('Souris-Red-Rainy Region … 1 of 3'). The biome colors appear only in the zoomed-out picture, and the watershed lines are still there.
findings.why: If Biomes doesn't draw at the bookmark's zoom, 'click the shading along the route' gives students a watershed or the purchase, and they can't answer 'Which biome covers the Great Plains?'
findings.suggestion: Check the Biomes layer's visible range and make sure it draws at the Up the Missouri bookmark; if it is limited by zoom, widen the range or have the sheet say 'zoom out until the colors appear'. Also check that turning off United States Watersheds hides all six of its sublayers.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biomes.png; --q3-biome-click.png; pop-up text 'Souris-Red-Rainy Region, HUC ID: 09' (1 of 3)

findings.where: Biomes pop-up (q3-biome-click); Q3 step 4
findings.what: Under the biome and ecoregion, the pop-up has the heading 'Nature Could Recover' and says the ecoregion 'would require restoration to reach Half Protected'.
findings.why: That's a conservation policy goal, not history or geography, and it has nothing to do with the Corps of Discovery. In my district a parent could read it as advocacy slipped into a history lesson, and I'd have to defend it.
findings.suggestion: Hide the conservation-status fields in this map's pop-up so it shows only the biome, realm and ecoregion.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q3-biome-click.png; pop-up text 'Nature Could Recover … would require restoration to reach Half Protected'

findings.where: Territorial acquisitions to 1803, Louisiana Purchase pop-up (q1-purchase); Q1 step 3 and the Looking back question
findings.what: The pop-up says the purchase 'encompassed 530,000,000 acres of territory … that the United States purchased from France'. The sheet is careful to say the United States bought France's claim and that Native nations governed most of the land. The pop-up isn't careful, and it has no source line.
findings.why: Students will quote the pop-up, and Looking back asks them whose land it was, so the pop-up undercuts the sheet. I'd also want a source for the 530 million acres and the $15 million.
findings.suggestion: Reword it as: 'In 1803 the United States paid France $15 million for its claim to about 530 million acres. Native nations lived on and governed most of this land.' Add a source line, such as the National Archives.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png; pop-up text 'The Louisiana Purchase encompassed 530,000,000 acres of territory in North America that the United States purchased from France in 1803 for $15 million.'

findings.where: Louisiana Purchase pop-up (q1-purchase); Q1 'About how much bigger did the country become?'
findings.what: The answer notes say the pop-up's Area in Square Kilometers field confirms the doubling, but the pop-up I see has only that one sentence and no area.
findings.why: Students have no numbers for 'how much bigger', so they judge by eye, and my answer key relies on a field they can't see.
findings.suggestion: Add the area, in square miles since that's what my students use, to both the 1783 and the 1803 pop-ups, or remove the reference from the answer notes.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png; pop-up text has no area field

findings.where: Territorial acquisitions to 1803 (open, q1-purchase); sheet Reading the map ('green is the land Britain gave up') and Q1 step 2
findings.what: The 1783 land is a dull gray-teal, not what I'd call green, and when I click the yellow purchase it turns bright green with the selection highlight. With the legend open, the panel covers most of the 1783 land.
findings.why: Students told 'green = 1783' will read the clicked purchase as the 1783 land, and they can't compare the two areas while the legend hides one of them.
findings.suggestion: Call the 1783 color gray-green or teal on the sheet, or recolor it a clear green, and use a selection highlight that isn't green (an outline only). Add 'Close the legend to compare' to Q1 step 2.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--open.png; --q1-purchase.png

findings.where: Lewis and Clark trail and campsites (open, q1-purchase, q3-biome-click); Q4 steps 3-4 (find the trail's eastern end at Pittsburgh and measure to the Pacific)
findings.what: The campsite dots are so close together that the purple trail line is hidden under them for most of the route. Past the trail's eastern end there are more scattered dots farther east, toward the Chesapeake. The map has no place names, so nothing marks Pittsburgh.
findings.why: Students will measure from the farthest-east dot instead of Pittsburgh and get a distance outside 2,100 to 2,300 miles.
findings.suggestion: Add labelled points 'Pittsburgh: trail begins' and 'Mouth of the Columbia River' at the two ends. Explain the eastern dots on the sheet or in the legend (I'd check what they are; perhaps Lewis's travel in 1803 before Pittsburgh). Draw the trail line above the campsites, or show fewer dots when zoomed out.
findings.evidence: louisiana-purchase-1803-1806--q1-purchase.png and --q3-biome-click.png (dots east of the trail's end); --open.png (line hidden under dots)

war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine.works: At The War of 1812 bookmark the three clusters of diamonds (Great Lakes, Chesapeake, Gulf) stand out, and the date in the New Orleans pop-up makes the after-Ghent point easy. The treaty-line and recognition pop-ups are precise and sourced (Avalon Project, Office of the Historian), and the sheet openly corrects the legend's 'British' label. That's the kind of care I can defend.

findings.where: Historic National Boundaries: 1800 with Battles of the War of 1812 (q1-bookmark, q2-neworleans); Q1 and Q2
findings.what: The pink 'United States' stops at the Mississippi. So New Orleans, the biggest American victory, sits in unshaded 'Louisiana' outside the United States, and so do the battles on the upper Mississippi. Yet the New Orleans pop-up calls it 'a critical American port'.
findings.why: Students will reasonably ask why the United States was defending a city the map puts outside the country, when Louisiana was a state by 1812. A map that contradicts its own pop-up is hard to defend.
findings.suggestion: Use boundaries from 1812 or 1815 for the battles, or add the Louisiana Purchase as part of the United States. At the least, add to the sheet's Reading the map: 'The pink shows 1800. By 1812 the United States also held the Louisiana Purchase, including New Orleans.'
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q1-bookmark.png; --q2-neworleans.png; pop-up text 'a critical American port'

findings.where: Battles of the War of 1812 legend and pop-up (open, q2-neworleans); sheet Reading the map ('the pop-up's leaders and story tell you who fought'); Q1, Q2
findings.what: The legend says 'British Victory' for every win by an opponent, so Fort Mims, a Red Stick Creek victory, shows as British. The sheet says the pop-up's leaders tell students who fought, but the New Orleans pop-up I opened has the date, 'American Side Victory', the casualties and a long story, and no leaders line.
findings.why: Labelling a Native nation's victory as British is factually wrong, and the only correction is buried in long story text. That's a point about Native nations a reviewer could raise.
findings.suggestion: Relabel the legend 'Victory for the United States', 'Victory for its opponents (Britain or Native nations)' and 'Inconclusive'. Add an 'Opponent:' line near the top of each pop-up (e.g. 'Opponent: Red Stick Creeks'). If a leaders field exists, check that it shows.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--open.png legend 'British Victory'; --q2-neworleans.png pop-up text (no leaders line)

findings.where: Battle pop-up (q2-neworleans); Q1 'In which three areas was most of the fighting?' and From the front step 3
findings.what: The answer notes say the pop-up gives a State Name field, but the pop-up I see doesn't name a state, and the map has no place names apart from country names such as 'United States'.
findings.why: Students who don't already know where the Great Lakes, the Chesapeake and the Gulf Coast are have nothing on the map to name the three areas, and my step 3 at the front ('read the State Name') fails.
findings.suggestion: Show the state or province with the battle name in the pop-up (e.g. 'New Orleans, Louisiana'), and check that the State Name field is included in the pop-up.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q2-neworleans.png; pop-up text 'New Orleans / January 8, 1815 / American Side Victory / Total Casualties: 2,096'

findings.where: Land Spain gave up in 1819, East Florida pop-up (q3-florida); Q3 step 3 (what did the United States gain from Spain)
findings.what: The pop-up says the Americans 'did agree to assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'.
findings.why: As I understand the treaty, the United States agreed to pay up to $5 million in claims that American citizens had against Spain, not damage Americans caused by rebelling. A wrong fact in a pop-up students copy is something I'd have to correct in front of the class. I'd check Article 11 of the treaty text; the Avalon Project link is already on the treaty-line pop-up.
findings.suggestion: If confirmed, reword it as: 'The United States did not pay Spain for the land. It agreed to pay up to $5 million in claims that American citizens had against Spain.' Add a source line and the missing final period. Consider adding one line of context on Jackson's 1818 campaign against the Seminoles in Spanish Florida.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-florida.png; pop-up text 'assume $5 million in damage caused by American citizens when they rebelled against Spain'

findings.where: The 1819 boundary bookmark with the legend open (q3-boundary) and zoomed out (q3-treatyline); Q3 steps 3-4 (click the green land, click each part of the line)
findings.what: At the bookmark, the legend panel covers Florida, the green land students are told to click, and the eastern end of the dashed line (parts 1 and 2, along the Sabine River). The only green in view is a small patch in the Rockies. The 'Land Spain gave up in 1819' legend heading shows, but its color swatches are cut off. Zoomed out, part 1 is a tiny stub right beside the big New Orleans diamond.
findings.why: Students will click the small western patch or never find Florida, and clicking part 1 can open the New Orleans battle instead.
findings.suggestion: Re-center The 1819 boundary bookmark farther east so that Florida and the Sabine stay clear of a right-hand legend. Add 'Close the legend' to Q3 step 3, and have students turn off Battles of the War of 1812 for Q3. I'd also check what the small green patch in the Rockies represents.
findings.evidence: war-of-1812-and-monroe-doctrine--q3-boundary.png; --q3-treatyline.png

findings.where: Latin American independence and US recognition at the Latin America in 1825 bookmark (q4-latin, q4-circle); Q4 step 3 (click the blue circles)
findings.what: A blue circle in southern Brazil sits right at the end of the label 'Paraguay 1811', and there's no 'Brazil 1822' label in view, so Paraguay looks as if it was recognized by 1824. Paraguay's own orange diamond sits next to the old 1800 country label 'Perú', and the Haiti diamond is half under the 'Federation of Central America 1821' label.
findings.why: Students who go by the labels will list Paraguay as recognized and miss Brazil. Q4 depends on matching the right names and dates.
findings.suggestion: Place each label clearly by its own symbol (e.g. above it, with a leader line), make sure Brazil's label shows at this bookmark with the legend open, and hide the 1800 country names in this view. Q4 step 3 could say 'read the nation's name in the pop-up title'.

findings.where: Battles legend (open), recognition pop-up (q4-circle) and New Orleans pop-up (q2-neworleans); Q2, Q4
findings.what: The casualties key ends with '< 0'. Recognition dates read '1/27/1823, 12:00 AM'. The New Orleans story repeats its last paragraph word for word and has no source line, though it includes judgments like 'a symbol of American democracy triumphing over the old European ideas of aristocracy and entitlement'.
findings.why: Each of these is small, but together they look careless. An interpretive sentence with no source in the pop-up is harder for me to defend than one credited to the American Battlefield Trust.
findings.suggestion: Change the smallest size key to the real minimum; show dates as 'January 27, 1823'; delete the repeated paragraph; and add 'Source: American Battlefield Trust' to each battle pop-up.
